q0137.short: "Left to right: reference clock into a phase-frequency detector; its UP and DOWN outputs drive a charge pump; that feeds a loop filter, an R–C network; the filter's control voltage drives the VCO, whose output is f out. A divide-by-N block takes f out and feeds it back to the second input of the PFD, closing the loop. I'd label f ref, UP/DOWN, the pump current, V control, f out and f out over N, and write f out equal

q0138.title: PLL locking too fast or too slow
q0138.short: "It's the loop bandwidth trade-off. Too fast, meaning wide bandwidth, and the output inherits reference and charge-pump noise multiplied by N, reference spurs, and may overshoot or even go unstable as the bandwidth nears the reference frequency. Too slow and the lock time gets long, so startup and frequency changes lag, and the loop can't suppress the VCO's own noise and drift, so jitter rises, and it can't track inp

q0139.title: Why a crushed clock window hurts
q0139.short: "I take the clock window as the time you have each cycle for launch, logic, setup, skew and jitter. If you crush it, with a faster clock, jitter, duty-cycle error or PLL overshoot, you get setup and hold violations and metastability in synchronous logic, minimum-pulse-width failures in flops and memories, SNR loss in ADCs through aperture jitter, and eye closure and bit errors in serial links and DDR. Circuits see th

q0140.title: What kind of load is a SoC/CPU?
q0140.short: "A SoC is best described as a capacitive, time-varying current sink. It's CMOS, so power goes into charging and discharging capacitance every cycle: \alpha C V^2 f. On average it looks resistive, like 17 milliohms for a 54 amp core, but that's just V over I, and it changes with the workload. It isn't really inductive. The inductance is in the package and board, and with fast current steps it causes droop, which is wh

q0141.title: Maximum power transfer condition
q0141.short: "Maximum power goes to the load when the load resistance equals the source resistance, or for AC when ZL = Zs^. The load power is Vs^2RL/(Rs+RL)^2, and setting the derivative to zero gives RL = Rs, with P{max} = Vs^2/(4Rs). The catch is that efficiency is only 50% at that point, so it's used in RF and signal chains, not in power supplies, where you want low source impedance instead."

q0142.title: Why many capacitors on a power rail
q0142.short: "They're decoupling capacitors, acting as local charge reservoirs so fast current bursts don't pull the rail down. There are many because a real capacitor has ESR and inductance, so each one is only a low impedance over a limited band, above its self-resonant frequency it looks like an inductor. Paralleling several small parts divides the inductance and gives low impedance out to hundreds of megahertz. One massive ca

q0143.title: What is bulk capacitance?
q0143.short: "Bulk capacitance is the large capacitance, tens to thousands of microfarads, at a board's power entry or a regulator's input or output. It's the local energy tank: it supplies load steps while the regulator catches up, smooths converter input ripple, and provides hold-up. You size it from C = I\Delta t/\Delta V or from energy. It's slow, though. Big capacitors are inductive above a few hundred kilohertz, so small ce

q0144.title: Inductive flyback and protection
q0144.short: "Inductive flyback is the voltage spike when you suddenly interrupt current through an inductor. Since v=L\,di/dt, the inductor forces the current to continue by driving its voltage as high as needed, up to kilovolts if there's no path. It's unwanted with relays, motors and solenoids, where it can kill the driver, so you add a freewheel diode, or a diode with a Zener or a TVS, or a snubber. It's wanted in boost and f

q0145.title: PWM and its characteristics
q0145.short: "PWM is switching a signal fully on and off at a fixed frequency and varying the on-time fraction, the duty cycle D. The average is D\cdot V, for example 1.5 V from a 5 V signal at 30%, but the RMS is V\sqrt D, which sets heating. A filter or a slow load averages it. The main benefit is efficiency, since the switch is either on or off. Frequency is the trade-off: higher means smaller filters but more switching loss a

q0146.title: Wide-bandgap semiconductors: SiC, GaN
q0146.short: "The main ones are silicon carbide and gallium nitride, with gallium oxide and diamond in research. Their wide bandgap gives a critical field about ten times silicon's, so the drift region can be much thinner. That gives much lower on-resistance for a given voltage, smaller capacitances and faster switching, so higher efficiency and frequency with smaller magnetics. SiC fits high voltage, GaN fits up to roughly 650 v

q0147.title: Ways to step voltage up or down
q0147.short: "To step down you can use a divider, a Zener, a linear regulator or LDO, or a buck converter. To step up, a boost converter, a charge pump, or a transformer-based converter; buck-boost and SEPIC when the input crosses the output. For a power rail you don't use a divider or Zener since the output moves with load and wastes power. You use an LDO when the drop and current are small and you want low noise, because effici

q0148.title: Why not a divider for a power rail
q0148.short: "A divider's output is a Thevenin source with output resistance R1\parallel R2, so the voltage drops with load current, and a rail's load changes all the time. To make it stiff you'd need tiny resistors that waste far more power than the load uses, and it still isn't regulated against input changes. For 5 V to 3.3 V at 20 mA it would burn watts for 66 milliwatts. Use an LDO or buck, which use feedback to hold the out

q0149.title: When a voltage divider is applicable
q0149.short: "A divider works when the load draws negligible current compared with the divider's own current, so the output is just the resistor ratio. Typical uses are regulator feedback networks, scaling a voltage into an ADC or comparator (ideally through a buffer), enable-pin under-voltage thresholds, and bias networks. Rule of thumb: the load should be about 100 times the Thevenin resistance for 1% error. Then pick the resis

q0150.title: Design a power supply
q0150.short: "I'd start with requirements: input range, outputs, currents, ripple, efficiency, environment. For 12 V to 3.3 V at 2 A I'd use a synchronous buck rather than an LDO, which would waste 17 W. At 500 kHz that gives about D = 0.275, an 8.2 µH inductor, about 40 µF of ceramic output capacitance, and a feedback divider for the 0.6 V reference. Then I'd add soft start, current limit, UVLO, thermal protection and input prot

q0151.title: Supply overshoot and undershoot
q0151.short: "Undershoot makes logic slower, because gate delay rises as the supply drops, so you get timing failures, brown-outs, bad memory writes and analogue errors. Overshoot stresses devices, since it can exceed absolute-maximum ratings, and it increases power as V^2. It's tolerable for loads with wide input range or their own regulation, like motors, heaters or LEDs, and for brief events within spec. Low-voltage digital co

q0152.title: Parameters to track in a supply
q0152.short: "I'd track output voltage and its regulation against load and line, ripple and noise, transient response and loop stability, then input and output voltage and current to get efficiency and loss, plus quiescent current and temperature. Beyond that, start-up behaviour like soft-start and inrush, and protection thresholds: current limit, under-voltage lockout, thermal shutdown and power-good. At runtime I'd monitor volt

q0153.title: Specs for buying or designing a supply
q0153.short: "I'd start from the load and spec the output voltage and tolerance, continuous and peak current, ripple and noise, regulation and transient response. Then efficiency including no-load power, the input range and surge/inrush behaviour, protections like over-current and over-temperature, thermal derating, and certifications and cost. I'd size continuous current at about 70-80% of the rating, cover the peak, and verify

q0154.title: Energy conservation in power design
q0154.short: "Energy conservation says input power equals output power plus losses, almost always heat: P{in}=P{out}+P{loss}. It's a tool and a goal. As a tool, it gives me unknown currents: a 90% efficient converter making 6.6 W from 12 V draws 0.61 A. As a goal, wasted energy is heat and battery life: an LDO from 12 to 3.3 V at 2 A wastes 17 W while a buck wastes under 1 W."

q0155.title: Solve for the missing V or I
q0155.short: "Output power equals efficiency times input power: V{out}I{out}=\eta V{in}I{in}. Solve for the missing one. With 12 V in at 0.5 A and 3.3 V out, the ideal output current is 12\times0.5/3.3=1.82 A, or 1.64 A at 90% efficiency. I'd state the efficiency assumption, check direction (buck raises current, boost lowers it, LDO keeps it the same) and flag any result that implies more than 100% efficiency."

q0156.title: Name some voltage regulators
q0156.short: "I'd group them by how they work. Linear regulators, like a 7805, LM317 or an LDO, burn the excess voltage as heat, so they're simple and quiet but only step down. Switching regulators use an inductor and a switch, buck to step down, boost to step up, buck-boost for both, flyback for isolation, and they hit roughly 90 percent efficiency. Charge pumps use capacitors to double or invert a voltage at low current. And sh

q0157.title: Buck converter vs LDO trade-offs
q0157.short: "An LDO burns the extra voltage as heat in a series pass element, so its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, and it only steps down. A buck switches and uses an inductor to transfer energy, so it's around 90 percent efficient regardless of the voltage drop. The trade is that the LDO is tiny, quiet and fast, while the buck needs an inductor, has ripple and EMI, and needs careful layout. Big drop or high current, buck;

q0158.title: When an LDO beats a buck
q0158.short: "An LDO is more efficient when the voltage drop is small or the load is tiny. Its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, so it beats a buck whenever that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, like 3.6 volts down to 3.3 at 92 percent. At very light loads, a buck's own quiescent current and switching overhead can exceed the load, so a nano-amp-class LDO can win. At a big drop and real current, the buck always wins."

q0159.title: AC-AC, AC-DC, DC-DC, DC-AC converters
q0159.short: "It's a grid by input and output. AC to AC is a transformer, variac, or TRIAC phase control. AC to DC is a rectifier, usually a diode bridge plus a filter capacitor, often with a PFC stage. DC to DC is linear regulators, charge pumps and switching converters like buck, boost and flyback. DC to AC is an inverter: an H-bridge or three-phase bridge with PWM. They chain: a wall adapter is AC-DC then DC-DC, and a motor dr

q0160.title: Bridge rectifier operation
q0160.short: "A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond: AC across one diagonal, load across the other. On one half-cycle two diodes conduct and on the other half-cycle the other two do, but current always goes through the load in the same direction, so you get the absolute value of the input, pulsating DC at twice the line frequency. Two diodes are in the path, so you lose about 1.4 volts, and you add a capacitor to smooth

q0161.title: Why step-down regulators dominate
q0161.short: "Because supplies are usually higher than what the chips need, and chips keep going lower in voltage to save CV-squared-f power. Distributing at a higher voltage also means less current and less I-squared-R loss, so you convert down at the point of load. Step-down converters are also simpler: a buck has continuous output current and no right-half-plane zero, while a boost has higher input current, a pulsed output and

q0162.title: Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement
q0162.short: "Efficiency is output power over input power, so it's the fraction of source energy that reaches the load; the rest is loss and becomes heat. I measure Vin, Iin, Vout and Iout together, with Kelvin sensing at the converter pins, an electronic load, and a warmed-up unit, and I sweep load and input voltage because efficiency is a curve. It matters for heat, battery life, size and cost, reliability, and regulations."

q0163.title: Pin, Pout, efficiency: find the third
q0163.short: "Efficiency is output power over input power. Given two, rearrange: eta is Pout over Pin; Pout is Pin times eta; Pin is Pout divided by eta. For example, 5 watts out at 90 percent needs 5.56 watts in, losing 0.56. Input must always be larger than output, and for cascaded stages you multiply the efficiencies."

q0164.title: Where lost power goes and why it hurts
q0164.short: "Lost power becomes heat. The energy not delivered to the load is dissipated in FET and inductor resistance, switching transitions, magnetic cores and the controller's bias. That raises junction temperature by loss times thermal resistance, which risks thermal shutdown and shortens component life, shifts parameters like on-resistance, wastes battery energy, and forces larger heatsinks and more cost. So I compute the

q0165.title: Quiescent current of a regulator
q0165.short: "Quiescent current is what a regulator draws from its input just to operate, with no load: the bias for the reference, error amp, feedback divider and control. For an LDO it's the ground-pin current. It matters because it never goes away: in a battery device that sleeps at microamps, it can dominate standby current and light-load efficiency. For example, 50 microamps on a coin cell kills standby life, so for always-o

q0166.title: Design a power architecture from a spec
q0166.short: "I'd clarify input range, accuracy, noise, sequencing and thermal limits first, then build a power budget. For a 12 volt input with 5, 3.3, 1.8 and 1 volt rails plus a clean analog 1.8, it's about 27 watts out. I'd use a buck on each rail, fed directly from the input, around 90 percent efficient overall, with a low-noise LDO from 3.3 volts for the analog rail. Then I'd check input current at minimum voltage, sizing,

q0167.title: Multiple output voltages from one supply
q0167.short: "Per-rail switching regulators are the default: bucks for rails below the input, boost or buck-boost for ones above, and an inverting converter or charge pump for negative rails. LDOs suit small, clean rails, but their input current equals output current, so cascading them doesn't cut total loss. For compact designs I'd use a PMIC, multi-output buck or SIMO converter, and for isolated or mains-fed rails a multi-windi

q0168.title: Same voltage, different noise rails
q0168.short: "I'd keep the noisy and quiet loads from sharing a path. The digital 3.3 V comes from a buck, and the analog 3.3 V comes from a low-noise LDO fed from a slightly higher rail, with an LC or ferrite filter if the LDO's PSRR at the switching frequency isn't enough. I'd compute the required attenuation from the ripple and the noise budget, damp any LC filter, and manage the switcher with frequency choice, sync or spread

q0169.title: Large dropout but clean, efficient rail
q0169.short: "A buck takes the big drop efficiently, down to just above the target, and then a low-noise LDO takes the last few hundred millivolts and cleans the rail. For 12 to 3.3 volts at an amp, the buck goes to about 3.6 volts and the LDO drops 0.3 volts, so it only dissipates 0.3 watts and the chain is around 84 percent efficient. I choose the headroom as the smallest value that still gives enough PSRR at the switching freq

q0170.title: Intermediate bus converter and when needed
q0170.short: "An intermediate bus converter is the first stage of a two-stage architecture: it steps a high input like 48 volts down to an intermediate bus like 12, often isolated and fixed-ratio, and point-of-load buck converters near each chip then make the final rails. It's needed because distributing at high voltage cuts I-squared-R loss, and because a single stage from 48 volts to 1 volt needs a duty cycle near 2 percent, wh

q0171.title: Power sequencing: why, order, timing
q0171.short: "Power sequencing is controlling the order and timing of supply rails turning on and off. It's needed because multi-rail chips can be damaged or left in undefined states if, say, the I/O is powered while the core isn't, since ESD diodes back-power the core or latch-up occurs. The order comes from the datasheets: sequence sections and absolute max ratings like I/O not exceeding core by 0.3 volts. The timing is usually

q0172.title: Implementing power sequencing
q0172.short: "The simplest is to chain regulators: the power-good pin of one, pulled up through a resistor, drives the enable of the next, so each rail starts only when the previous is valid. For extra delay I add an RC on the enable, with t=RC\ln[V{cc}/(V{cc}-V{th})], though tolerance is loose. For more control I use a voltage supervisor, or a sequencer IC or PMIC, or an MCU or CPLD reading PGs. Tracking pins and load switches h

q0173.title: What is a buck converter
q0173.short: "A buck converter is an efficient switching regulator that steps a voltage down. A transistor chops the input on and off at a fixed frequency, and an inductor and capacitor average it, so the output is the input times the duty cycle. A feedback loop adjusts the duty cycle to hold the output constant. It's efficient because the switch is either fully on or fully off, so almost no power is lost, unlike a linear regulat

q0174.title: How a buck converter works
q0174.short: "A buck has two states. When the high-side switch is on, the inductor sees V{in}-V{out} and its current ramps up while feeding the load. When the switch turns off, the inductor current keeps flowing through the diode or low-side FET, the inductor sees -V{out}, and the current ramps down. The output capacitor smooths the ripple. In steady state the up and down ramps balance, so V{out}=D\,V{in}. A feedback loop adjusts

q0175.title: Draw a buck converter circuit
q0175.short: "I'd draw the input source with a capacitor across it, then a high-side NFET from the input rail to a switch node. From the switch node, a diode down to ground with the cathode at the node, and an inductor going right to the output. At the output, a capacitor to ground in parallel with the load. A feedback divider goes back to the controller, which drives the FET gate with PWM. For a synchronous buck I replace the di

q0176.title: Buck converter applications
q0176.short: "Bucks are everywhere you need an efficient step-down: point-of-load rails like 12 V or 5 V down to 3.3 V, 1.8 V or 1 V for processors, FPGAs and memory; battery-powered devices where efficiency sets runtime; automotive and industrial buses stepped down to logic rails; and CPU core rails, which are multiphase bucks. The same stage regulates current for LED drivers and chargers. I'd use an LDO instead for tiny dropout

q0177.title: SIMO buck converter
q0177.short: "SIMO means single-inductor multiple-output: one input, one shared inductor, several regulated rails. The inductor is time-multiplexed: it's charged from the input and then dumped into one output at a time, usually in discontinuous mode so each slot starts at zero current. The win is area and cost, because one inductor replaces several. The costs are cross-regulation between outputs, high peak inductor currents, a sh

q0178.title: What sets a buck's output voltage
q0178.short: "In the power stage, the duty cycle and input set the output: V{out}=D\,V{in} in continuous conduction, because the inductor can't sustain a DC voltage, so the average switch-node voltage must equal V{out}. In a real regulator the feedback loop picks D: a divider scales V{out} to a reference, and the loop adjusts D until they match, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). The formula changes with losses and in discontinuous mode.

q0179.title: What is duty cycle
q0179.short: "Duty cycle is the fraction of each switching period that the switch is on: D=t{on}/T, between 0 and 100 percent. It's independent of frequency: at 500 kHz, 27.5 percent is a 550 ns on-time. In a buck the switch node is a pulse train whose average is D\,V{in}, so duty cycle sets the output voltage, and the feedback loop adjusts it to regulate."

q0180.title: How to calculate duty cycle
q0180.short: "Ideally, duty cycle is V{out}/V{in}, so 12 V to 3.3 V is 27.5 percent. In a real converter I add the drops: for a synchronous buck D=\frac{V{out}+I(R{ls}+R{DCR})}{V{in}-I(R{hs}-R{ls})}, which at 2 A is about 28 percent, and with a Schottky diode closer to 30.7 percent. I can also read it from the scope as on-time over period, or get it from I{in}/I{out}. All of that assumes continuous conduction."

q0181.title: Buck at 100% and 0% duty
q0181.short: "At 100 percent duty the high-side is always on, there's no switching or ripple, and V{out} is the input minus the drops across the switch and inductor, so the converter is in dropout and not regulating. At 0 percent the high-side is always off, the inductor current ramps down at V{out}/L, and the output decays; in a forced-PWM synchronous buck the current even reverses and feeds energy back to the input. In real par

q0182.title: Duty cycle from a Vout/Vin ratio
q0182.short: "For a buck in continuous conduction, duty cycle equals the ratio: D=V{out}/V{in}, from volt-second balance. A ratio of 0.275 is 27.5 percent, which at 500 kHz is a 550 ns on-time. I'd check that against the minimum on-time. It's a bit higher with real drops, and in discontinuous mode at light load the ratio alone isn't enough: D=M\sqrt{K/(1-M)} with K=2L/(RT)."

q0183.title: Vout from duty cycle and Vin
q0183.short: "Yes, in continuous conduction: V{out}=D\,V{in}, so 27.5 percent of 12 V is 3.3 V. Real drops pull it down a bit. In discontinuous mode at light load the output is higher for the same duty cycle, so I'd need the load, inductance and frequency too. And in a closed-loop regulator, D isn't an independent input; the feedback loop sets it to hold V{out}."

q0184.title: DC load-line and its tradeoffs
q0184.short: "A DC load line, or droop, is a deliberate drop in output voltage with load current: V{out}=V{ref}-R{LL}I{out}, made by sensing current and subtracting it from the setpoint. It lets the output use the whole tolerance window during a load step instead of half, so you need less output capacitance and see less overshoot, and the load runs at lower voltage and power when busy. The costs are worse DC accuracy, a lower vol

q0185.title: Draw all the buck waveforms
q0185.short: "Switch node is a 12 V pulse that sits at about minus a diode drop when off, averaging 3.3 V. Inductor voltage is that minus V{out}: plus 8.7 V then minus 3.3 V. Integrate it and the inductor current is a triangle about 1 A peak to peak around 2 A. The capacitor current is that triangle with the load average removed, so its integral is a small parabolic ripple of ten-ish millivolts. Input current is the inductor curr

q0186.title: Purpose of output inductor and capacitor
q0186.short: "The inductor stores energy and releases it, so the chopped 12 V pulse becomes a smooth current without burning power; it's the lossless alternative to a series resistor. The capacitor absorbs the inductor's current ripple and holds the output voltage steady, and it supplies load steps until the inductor catches up. Together they're a second-order low-pass with a corner well below the switching frequency, here 16 kHz

q0187.title: Inductor and capacitor current directions
q0187.short: "The inductor current flows from the switch node toward the output in both states; it ramps up when the high-side FET is on and the current comes from the input, and it ramps down during the off state, with the current coming up through the diode or low-side FET from ground. The capacitor current is iL minus the load current, so it's positive, charging, when the inductor current is above the average and negative, dis

q0188.title: Why inductor current is a linear ramp
q0188.short: "It follows from v = L\,di/dt. In the on state the inductor sees roughly V{in}-V{out}, constant, so the current rises linearly with slope (V{in}-V{out})/L. In the off state it sees -V{out}, constant, so it falls linearly at V{out}/L. The slope depends only on those voltages and L, not on the load; the load just sets the average of the triangle. It's only approximately linear, assuming small ripple and negligible resi

q0189.title: Is the output capacitor voltage a linear ramp
q0189.short: "A constant capacitor current gives a linear ramp, but in a buck the capacitor current is a triangle, the inductor current minus the load. The integral of a triangle is a parabola, so the capacitor voltage is made of parabolic arcs, with its extremes where the capacitor current crosses zero. It only looks like a linear ramp when ESR dominates, because the ESR drop follows the current. Ripple is about \Delta I/(8fC),

q0190.title: When the output capacitor charges and discharges
q0190.short: "The capacitor charges when the inductor current is above the load current and discharges when it's below, because the capacitor current is just inductor current minus load current. In steady state that's the top half and bottom half of the inductor triangle, not the on and off states: the capacitor starts charging halfway up the on ramp and stops halfway down the off ramp, and charging lasts exactly half a period. I

q0191.title: Inductor voltage polarity in a buck
q0191.short: "With the current flowing from the switch node to the output, the voltage across the inductor is positive on the switch-node end during the on state, plus 8.7 V in my example, and the current ramps up as it stores energy. In the off state the high-side FET opens, the inductor keeps its current, so its polarity reverses: the switch-node end goes negative relative to the output, minus 3.3 V, and the current ramps down

q0192.title: When the inductor sinks and supplies current
q0192.short: "The inductor current always flows toward the output, so I think in power terms. During the on state the input is connected, the inductor has 8.7 V across it and rising current, so it absorbs energy, it's sinking power from the input. During the off state the input is disconnected and the inductor's voltage reverses, so it delivers its stored energy to the output, supplying the load. In steady state those energies ma

q0193.title: Why a buck needs an input capacitor
q0193.short: "The buck draws pulsed current from the input, only while the high-side FET is on, with a small average and tall pulses. A real source and its wiring have inductance and can't supply those fast pulses, so the input capacitor sits at the FET as a local reservoir, supplying the pulses and getting recharged smoothly. Without it the input would droop and ring, the switch node could overshoot beyond the FET rating, EMI wo

q0194.title: Voltage and current ripple from circuit analysis
q0194.short: "Ripple is the peak-to-peak switching-frequency variation of the inductor current and the output voltage. The inductor current ramps by V\cdot t/L each state, so \Delta I=V{out}(1-D)/(Lf), about 1 A in my example. The capacitor sees that as a triangle with zero average, so the capacitive voltage ripple is \Delta I/(8fC), about 11.6 mV, plus \Delta I\cdot ESR. Bigger L, higher f, bigger C and lower ESR all reduce it,

q0195.title: What sets the inductor current slope
q0195.short: "The slope is the voltage across the inductor divided by L. In the on state that's (V{in}-V{out})/L, rising 1.85 A/µs in my 12 V to 3.3 V, 4.7 µH example, and in the off state it's -V{out}/L, falling 0.7 A/µs. The load current doesn't change the slope, only the offset; the duty cycle only decides how long you stay on each one. In real parts, resistive drops, diode drop, tolerance and saturation modify it slightly."

q0196.title: What sets output capacitor voltage slope
q0196.short: "The slope is iC/C. In a buck the capacitor current is the inductor current minus the load current, a triangle of plus and minus half the ripple current, so the voltage slope swings between about minus and plus 23 mV/µs in my example (0.51 A over 22 µF) and is zero at the ripple extremes. So the ripple current and C set it. In a load step it is \Delta I/C, and at start-up the soft-start ramp times C sets the inrush."

q0197.title: Why the buck needs a diode
q0197.short: "The diode is the freewheeling path. When the high-side FET opens, the inductor current can't stop, so the inductor forces the switch node negative until something conducts. The diode does that at about minus 0.4 V and lets the current ramp down through the load. Without it the node would fly down until the FET avalanches or the controller's switch pin breaks: in my example the inductor holds about 15 µJ at turn-off,

q0198.title: Buck with an ideal diode
q0198.short: "An ideal diode removes the forward-drop loss: for 12 V to 3.3 V at 2 A with a 0.5 V Schottky that's 0.73 W of 6.6 W, so efficiency goes from about 90% toward 100%, and the gain is bigger at lower output voltages. It also makes the off-state switch node exactly 0 V, the duty cycle exactly V{out}/V{in}, and removes reverse-recovery spikes. What it doesn't change is that it can't conduct backwards, so you still get DCM

q0199.title: Switch node voltage in the off state
q0199.short: "Just below ground: the inductor current keeps flowing, so the switch node is pulled down until the freewheel path conducts. With a Schottky that's about minus 0.4 V; with a synchronous low-side FET it's minus I\,R{ds(on)}, tens of millivolts, with brief dips to about minus 0.7 V in dead time on the body diode. The one exception is DCM: after the inductor current hits zero the node floats and rings around V{out}."

q0200.title: Source of inductor current in the off state
q0200.short: "By KCL at the switch node, with the high-side FET open the inductor current has to come through the diode, or the low-side FET, from ground. So it circulates: ground, diode, switch node, inductor, load, back to ground; the input isn't in the loop. The energy comes from the inductor's magnetic field, built up during the on time, about 9.6 µJ per cycle in my example. The capacitor only fills in the gap when the induct

q0201.title: Buck power bridge type and why
q0201.short: "Most buck converters use a half bridge of two NFETs with synchronous rectification: a high-side NFET to V{in} and a low-side NFET to ground, driven complementary with dead time. The low-side FET replaces the diode because I\cdot R{DS(on)} is far below a diode's fixed 0.3 to 0.7 V drop, which matters most at low output voltage and high current. NFETs on both sides because electrons are more mobile than holes, so an N

q0202.title: Freewheel diode: why and what if removed
q0202.short: "The diode is the freewheel path. When the high-side switch opens, the inductor current can't jump, so the switch node swings negative until the diode turns on at about minus 0.4 V and carries the current while it decays. Remove it and the inductor generates whatever voltage it needs, L\,di/dt, so SW slams negative at around 10 V per nanosecond until some FET or pin avalanches. That dumps the inductor's stored energy

q0203.title: Synchronous rectification pros and cons
q0203.short: "Synchronous rectification replaces the freewheel diode with a low-side MOSFET driven complementary to the high side. It wins on efficiency: loss is I^2R{DS(on)} instead of Vf\cdot I, so at 3.3 V out and 2 A you cut roughly 650 mW to about 30 mW. The costs are a second gate driver, dead time to avoid shoot-through with body-diode loss during it, gate-drive power at all loads, and negative inductor current at light lo

q0204.title: High-side NFET vs PFET trade-offs
q0204.short: "An NFET is the better switch and a PFET is the easier one to drive. NFETs have two to three times lower R{DS(on)} per area because electrons are more mobile than holes, so less gate charge and capacitance and lower cost, but a high-side NFET needs its gate above V{in}, so a bootstrap or charge pump, and it can't reach 100% duty without refresh. A high-side PFET just pulls its gate down relative to V{in} and supports

q0205.title: Symmetrical power bridge pros and cons
q0205.short: "I'd take symmetrical to mean two identical FETs in the half bridge. Pros: one part number, identical drive and timing, and bidirectional capability, so it's good near 50% duty and for inverters or bidirectional converters. Con: in a buck the high side conducts D and hard-switches while the low side conducts 1-D with near-zero-voltage switching, so equal sizing wastes silicon at small duty. For fixed area the optimal

q0206.title: Design a high-side NFET drive
q0206.short: "The high-side NFET's source is the switch node, so its gate has to go to V{in} plus about 5 V. I'd use a bootstrap: a gate driver whose supply pin is a capacitor from BST to SW, charged through a Schottky from a 5 V rail while the low side is on. Size it as C\ge Qg/\Delta V, for example 12 nC over 0.3 V is 40 nF, then use 100 nF. Considerations: refresh limits max duty, pre-biased start-up, SW undershoot and dv/dt i

q0207.title: Shoot-through and dead time
q0207.short: "If both are on, V{in} is shorted to ground through two small R{DS(on)}s. Real current is tens to hundreds of amps for nanoseconds, limited by saturation and the input cap, but it wastes energy every cycle, heats the FETs, droops V{in} and can destroy them. Avoid it with dead time, ideally adaptive, or non-overlapping gate logic. Also guard against dv/dt-induced turn-on through the Miller capacitance with a low-imped

q0208.title: Body diode in the off state, SW waveform
q0208.short: "In the off state the inductor current keeps flowing through the low side. During the dead time both FETs are off, so it flows through the low-side body diode and SW sits about one diode drop, 0.7 to 1 V, below ground. Then the low-side channel turns on and SW comes up to about minus I\,R{DS(on)}, tens of millivolts. Before the high side turns on there's another dead-time shelf. When the high side turns on the diode

q0209.title: Design considerations from body diode behavior
q0209.short: "The body diode conducts in dead time at about 0.7 to 1 V and then must be forced off by the high-side turn-on. So I'd budget its conduction loss V{SD}Itdf and its recovery loss Q{rr}V{in}f, set dead time as short as is safe, probably adaptive, check the negative SW voltage against the controller's rating, watch the recovery spike and ringing for EMI and overshoot, check the diode's current and thermal rating, and ch

q0210.title: Reducing body diode effects
q0210.short: "Attack each mechanism. Shorten the dead time with adaptive control so the diode conducts as little as possible, which cuts both conduction and stored charge. Add a Schottky in parallel, but only co-packaged or monolithic, since nanohenries of loop inductance stop it taking the current. Choose a FET with low Q{rr} and soft recovery. Slow the high-side turn-on or add a snubber and tighten the layout to tame the recove

q0211.title: Why buck beats LDO efficiency
q0211.short: "An LDO is a series resistor: all the output current passes through it and it burns (V{in}-V{out})\times I{out}, so efficiency is about V{out}/V{in}, 27% for 12 V to 3.3 V. A buck uses switches that are either fully on or fully off, so they dissipate almost nothing, plus an inductor and capacitor that store and return energy instead of dissipating it. Power is conserved, so the input current drops to D\cdot I{out}. R

q0212.title: Sizing L and C for ripple spec
q0212.short: "Size the inductor from the ripple current: L=\dfrac{V{out}(1-D)}{f\,\Delta I} with \Delta I about 30% of full load. Then the output capacitor from \Delta V\approx\dfrac{\Delta I}{8fC}+\Delta I\cdot ESR, so C\ge\dfrac{\Delta I}{8f(\Delta V-\Delta I\cdot ESR)}. For 12 V to 3.3 V, 3 A, 600 kHz, 20 mV: 4.7 µH and about 10 µF effective, so 22 µF nominal after ceramic derating. Then check the inductor's saturation current

q0213.title: Component-by-component loss and ripple
q0213.short: "I'd go part by part. The high-side FET has conduction loss D\,I^2R and the largest switching loss; the low-side FET has the largest conduction loss plus dead-time and recovery loss; the driver adds QgVf and quiescent current; the inductor loses in DCR and core and sets the ripple current; the output capacitor barely affects efficiency but sets the voltage ripple through C and ESR; the input capacitor carries pulsed

q0214.title: Ways to increase buck efficiency
q0214.short: "First I'd find the dominant loss. At heavy load it's conduction, so lower-R{DS(on)} FETs (low side first), a lower-DCR inductor and, at high current, multiphase. For switching loss, lower the frequency with a bigger inductor, pick low-Qg/low-Q{rr} FETs, tune dead time adaptively and trade edge speed against EMI. At light load use PFM or diode emulation and low quiescent current. And if possible lower V{in}, since sw

q0215.title: Ways to decrease buck ripple
q0215.short: "Output ripple is \Delta IL/(8fC)+\Delta IL\cdot ESR with \Delta IL=V{out}(1-D)/(Lf), so increase L, C or f, or reduce ESR. Frequency is the strongest lever: the capacitive ripple goes as 1/f^2. Beyond that, interleave multiple phases to cancel ripple current and raise its frequency, add a second-stage LC or ferrite-bead filter, or a post-LDO. High-frequency spikes need layout and local small capacitors, not more bul

q0216.title: Switching frequency vs efficiency and ripple
q0216.short: "Higher switching frequency lowers ripple and shrinks L and C: inductor ripple current goes as 1/f and the capacitor ripple as 1/f^2. But overlap, C{oss}, gate-drive, dead-time and recovery losses all scale with f, so efficiency drops. With a fixed inductor, efficiency peaks at a moderate frequency (about 300 kHz in my example) because lower ripple current also cuts RMS and core loss. With the inductor scaled to hold

q0217.title: Biggest efficiency loss sources in a buck
q0217.short: "At nominal load: the low-side FET (conducts 1-D of the cycle, so the biggest I^2R), then the high-side FET (conduction plus all the hard switching loss), then the inductor (DCR plus core). Capacitors and feedback are negligible. In a 12 V to 3.3 V, 2 A example, about 180, 140 and 120 mW of 457 mW. The ranking shifts: at light load fixed losses (gate drive, recovery, quiescent) dominate; at high V{in} or high frequen

q0218.title: Why reduce output ripple
q0218.short: "Ripple uses up the load's supply tolerance and couples into sensitive circuits: ADC noise, VCO and PLL spurs, audio and sensor error, through finite PSRR that gets worse at high frequency. It also means higher peak and RMS current, more inductor core loss, capacitor heating and conducted EMI. For example, 10 mV of ripple on a VCO with 5 MHz/V pushing gives about a -26 dBc spur before filtering. But reducing it costs

q0219.title: When ripple matters less
q0219.short: "Ripple matters less when the load tolerates it or doesn't see it: a digital rail with plus or minus 10% tolerance, a load behind an LDO or filter with good rejection at f{sw}, or loads that average it, such as heaters, motor windings, and LEDs driven at average current. Then I'd raise the ripple ratio, using a smaller inductor and capacitor for lower cost and faster transients, while still checking peak current, EMI

q0220.title: Switching frequency upper and lower limits
q0220.short: "Upper limit: switching loss scales with frequency, the pulse can't be shorter than the minimum on-time (f{max}=D/t{on,min}, 2 MHz for 12 V to 1.2 V with 50 ns), plus core loss, EMI and edge times. Lower limit: L and C scale as 1/f, so 1 A and 10 mV at 20 kHz needs 120 µH and 625 µF, the loop crossover must stay below f{sw}/10, and below 20 kHz it's audible. At 1 THz the period is 1 ps, shorter than any FET edge; at

q0221.title: How switching frequency affects performance
q0221.short: "Higher switching frequency means less ripple and smaller inductors and capacitors, and it lets the loop be faster. The cost is that every per-cycle loss, like gate charge, switch-node capacitance and transition overlap, scales linearly with frequency, so efficiency and heat get worse. It also pushes against the minimum on-time limit for big step-downs and moves your EMI harmonics around. So you pick a frequency that

q0222.title: Dropout, Vin, Vout, Iout effects on a regulator
q0222.short: "Dropout is the minimum headroom between input and output an LDO needs to regulate, about load current times pass-device resistance. For an LDO, efficiency is V{out}/V{in} and PSRR collapses near dropout. A buck has the equivalent as a maximum duty cycle limit, where it needs about V{out} plus I\cdot(R{on}+DCR). In a buck, more V{in} means more ripple and more switching loss; more V{out} helps efficiency; and output

q0223.title: Output voltage sensing and feedback network
q0223.short: "The output voltage is sensed with a resistor divider into the feedback pin. The error amp compares that pin to an internal reference, usually around 0.6 to 1 V, and the loop adjusts the duty cycle until they match, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). The divider is needed because the reference is lower than the output and because it lets you program the rail with two resistors. There's usually a feed-forward cap across the t

q0224.title: Feedback divider resistance too high or too low
q0224.short: "Too high, and the feedback pin's bias current flows through the top resistor and shifts the output, leakage and noise pickup get worse, and the resistance plus pin capacitance makes a pole that can eat phase margin. Too low, and the divider itself draws current all the time, which hurts efficiency at light load and battery life. So you pick something in the tens to hundreds of kΩ, within the datasheet's recommendati

q0225.title: Ways to sense output current
q0225.short: "The simplest is a series sense resistor with a current-sense amplifier: accurate, but it costs I^2R loss. To avoid the loss, converters sense the inductor's DCR with an RC network (time constant L/DCR) or the MOSFET's R{DS(on)} while it's on, or use a SenseFET mirror, but those drift with temperature. For isolation or high current you use a Hall sensor or a current transformer."

q0226.title: Where to sense buck output current
q0226.short: "For control and fast protection I sense the inductor or switch current, before the output capacitor, because that's the real state of the power stage and it isn't filtered yet. For accurate load current or telemetry I sense after the capacitor in series with the load, where it's smooth DC and the common-mode is just V{out}. Sensing right after the inductor still shows the ripple. And the input side is for input curr

q0227.title: Signals used in the buck control loop
q0227.short: "The key one is V{out} through the feedback divider into the error amplifier, which sets the duty cycle. In current-mode control the inductor current is the inner loop and also gives cycle-by-cycle limiting. V{in} is used for feed-forward in voltage mode and for UVLO. Switch-node or low-side current detects zero crossing for light-load modes, and temperature, bias voltage and a power-good window on V{out} cover prote

q0228.title: Buck operating modes (CCM, DCM, PFM)
q0228.short: "There are two axes. Inductor current: continuous (CCM), where it never hits zero; discontinuous (DCM), where it returns to zero and rests; and forced CCM, where a synchronous low side lets it go negative. Modulation: PWM, fixed frequency with varying duty, and PFM or burst mode, fixed-size pulses at a rate set by the load. Real converters switch between them automatically: CCM-PWM at heavy load, DCM in the middle, P

q0229.title: DCM vs CCM in a buck converter
q0229.short: "In CCM the inductor current never reaches zero; in DCM it falls to zero and rests for part of the cycle, so there are three switching states instead of two. The boundary is at I{out}=\Delta IL/2. In CCM the output is D\,V{in} regardless of load; in DCM the gain depends on the load, so the duty cycle must shrink as the load drops. DCM also has higher peak current, ringing at the idle interval, and a more first-order

q0230.title: Improving buck efficiency at light load
q0230.short: "At light load the losses that don't scale with load, gate drive, switch-node capacitance and quiescent current, dominate the efficiency number. So you cut them: use PFM or burst mode so pulses and switching losses scale with load, diode emulation so you don't circulate reverse current, a low-quiescent-current controller and a high-value feedback divider, and in multiphase designs shed phases. At microamp loads an ul

q0231.title: Explain PFM operation in a buck
q0231.short: "PFM is a light-load mode where the converter fires fixed-size pulses only when the output droops below a threshold. Each pulse ramps the inductor to a fixed peak, then it discharges to zero into the output, and the converter sleeps until the output sags again. Pulse rate is proportional to load, so switching losses scale down with the load and efficiency stays high. The trade-offs are more, lower-frequency ripple an

q0232.title: PFM versus PWM in buck converters
q0232.short: "PWM keeps the frequency fixed and varies the pulse width; PFM keeps the pulse size fixed and varies how often it fires. PWM gives a clean fixed-frequency spectrum, low ripple and fast response, but poor light-load efficiency because it switches constantly. PFM scales switching losses with load so it's efficient at light load, but has larger low-frequency ripple, smeared EMI and a slower response to load steps. ICs c

q0233.title: Output ripple in PFM versus PWM
q0233.short: "PWM ripple is small and at the switching frequency: in CCM about \Delta IL/(8Cf) plus ESR, and it shrinks further in DCM as the pulses get shorter. PFM ripple comes from a fixed-size charge packet each pulse, about Q/C, which doesn't shrink with load; it just occurs less often. So at light load PFM ripple is roughly ten times PWM's, similar to full-load PWM in amplitude, but at a low and variable frequency that can

q0234.title: Inductor current in PFM mode
q0234.short: "In PFM the inductor current is a train of triangular pulses with zero current in between. Each pulse ramps up at (V{in}-V{out})/L to a fixed peak, ramps back down at V{out}/L to zero, where the low side shuts off. Then the inductor sits idle while the capacitor feeds the load. The pulse shape doesn't change with load, only how often they occur. Peak current is much higher than the average, and near half the peak the

q0235.title: Inductor and capacitor cycle in PFM
q0235.short: "Asleep, the capacitor feeds the load and the output droops. When it hits the threshold, the high-side FET turns on, the inductor current ramps up and stores energy; once it exceeds the load current the capacitor charges. Then the low side takes over, the inductor releases its energy into the output as the current ramps down, and the capacitor keeps charging until the inductor current drops below the load. At zero cu

q0236.title: What a multiphase buck is
q0236.short: "A multiphase buck is N buck power stages that share one output capacitor and one load but switch at evenly staggered times, 360 over N degrees apart. Each phase carries about one N-th of the current. The inductor currents add at the output and their ripples partly cancel, so the capacitor sees much less ripple, at N times the switching frequency. That lets you deliver high current, respond quickly to load steps and

q0237.title: Multiphase vs single-phase trade-offs
q0237.short: "Multiphase gives you more current, lower and higher-frequency output ripple, a faster transient response because the effective inductance is L over N, and heat spread over several stages. The costs are more parts and area, a more complex controller with current balancing, fixed losses that multiply with the phase count, and a harder layout. At the same total silicon the conduction loss doesn't change, so I'd pick mu

q0238.title: How multiphase bucks work and their challenges
q0238.short: "A multiphase buck has one voltage loop that sets total current and a PWM generator that gives each phase a staggered pulse. The main challenge is current sharing: the phases are connected through milliohms, so a 0.1 percent duty error at 12 V can push about 3 amps into one phase. So the controller senses each phase current, usually through the inductor DCR, and trims duty to balance. Other challenges are small sense

q0239.title: When to use a multiphase buck
q0239.short: "I'd use a multiphase buck when one stage can't meet the current, transient or thermal requirements: high current, typically tens of amps or more, at low voltage like a processor core; tough load steps where I need a small effective inductance; and limits on heat or component height. I'd choose the number of phases from the largest of current over derated per-phase rating, slew needed over slew per phase, and thermal

q0240.title: How multiphase increases output current
q0240.short: "The phase inductor currents all feed the same output node, so by KCL they add: four phases at 15 A each deliver 60 A. Each stage only needs FETs, an inductor and a package rated for its own share, so the single-stage limits go away. In practice the total is N times the derated phase limit divided by one plus the sharing error, and I'd check inductor peak current against saturation and think about what happens if one

q0241.title: Multiphase impact on efficiency
q0241.short: "Multiphase efficiency depends on the loss. Conduction loss is I^2R: with the same per-phase parts it falls as 1 over N, but for the same total silicon it is unchanged. Switching loss in total is about the same. Gate drive, driver quiescent and core loss grow with the number of phases, so at light load a multiphase buck is less efficient unless it sheds phases. So it's better at high load and needs phase shedding to

q0242.title: Multiphase and heat density
q0242.short: "Heat density is watts per area, and it is what limits a part. A single-phase 60 amp converter puts all its loss, around 5 watts at 1 volt, into one pair of FETs and one inductor. With four phases, each stage dissipates about a quarter of that, so temperature rise, which is power times thermal resistance, drops several-fold per package, and the heat is spread over more board. It's not exactly one over N because neigh

q0243.title: Multiphase and transient response
q0243.short: "A multiphase buck responds faster for two reasons. When the load steps, all phases ramp together, so the effective inductance is L over N and the total current slews N times faster, so the capacitor has to cover a much shorter gap. q0244.title: What stability means in a buck
q0244.short: "Stability means disturbances like load steps and noise die out instead of growing. In the small-signal model, that means all closed-loop poles are in the left half-plane. In practice I check the loop gain on a Bode plot: at the crossover frequency where gain is 0 dB, the phase margin should be about 45 to 60 degrees, and the gain margin 6 to 10 dB or more. q0245.title: Stable, marginal and unstable bucks
q0245.short: "Stable: a load step gives a dip and a damped recovery, and the ringing is at about the crossover frequency. Marginally stable: zero phase margin, poles on the imaginary axis, so a constant-amplitude oscillation. Unstable: poles in the right half-plane, so the oscillation grows until the duty cycle clamps or the current limit trips, which stresses the parts. q0246.title: The output LC filter as a system
q0246.short: "It's a second-order, linear low-pass filter: an inductor and capacitor give two poles at the resonant frequency 1 over 2 pi root LC. q0247.title: How L and C values affect stability
q0247.short: "L and C set the LC resonance, f0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}), and its Q. In voltage mode the compensator zeros are placed around that resonance, so bigger L or C moves it below the zeros and costs phase margin, while smaller values move it toward crossover and can push the peak through 0 dB. q0248.title: What happens in a load transient
q0248.short: "When the load steps up, the inductor current can't jump, since it only ramps at V in minus V out over L, so the output capacitor supplies the extra current. You see an immediate ESR step, then the capacitor droops at delta I over C. The loop senses the droop, raises the duty cycle, and the inductor ramps up until its current matches the new load, at which point the droop bottoms out. The inductor then overshoots sli

q0249.title: Characterizing transient response
q0249.short: "I characterize it in the time domain with a load step of defined size and slew rate: peak undershoot and overshoot, recovery time to a stated band like plus or minus one percent, and ringing, which gives the damping. In the frequency domain I measure the loop gain by injection to get crossover and phase and gain margin, and I look at closed-loop output impedance against the target impedance, delta V allowed over del

q0250.title: Feedforward capacitor in a buck
q0250.short: "A feedforward capacitor goes across the upper feedback resistor. At DC it does nothing, but at higher frequency it bypasses R1, giving a zero at 1 over 2 pi R1 Cff and a pole at 1 over 2 pi R1-parallel-R2 times Cff. q0251.title: Buck control topologies compared
q0251.short: "I group buck control by when the controller decides to switch. Voltage mode compares an error amplifier output to a fixed ramp: simple and quiet, but a second-order plant needs type III compensation. Current mode adds an inner inductor-current loop, which makes the plant first-order, rejects line changes and gives cycle-by-cycle current limit, but needs slope compensation and is noise-sensitive. q0252.title: Voltage mode vs current mode control
q0252.short: "Voltage mode has one loop: the error amplifier output is compared to a fixed ramp to set duty, and the plant is the full second-order LC, so it needs type III compensation. q0253.short: "Subharmonic oscillation is a cycle-by-cycle instability in fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. q0254.title: Peak current mode below and above 50% duty
q0254.short: "In peak current mode a disturbance, like noise tripping the comparator early or a load step, shows up as a current error that flips sign each cycle and is multiplied by D over one minus D. q0255.title: Slope compensation and when it's needed

q0270.title: What a boost converter is
q0270.short: "A boost converter is a switching regulator whose output is higher than its input, built from an inductor, a switch, a diode and a capacitor. q0271.short: "With the switch on, the inductor sits across V{in}, current ramps up at V{in}/L, the diode blocks, and the output capacitor feeds the load. q0273.short: "Anywhere the source is below the rail you need. q0275.short: "The inductor is the energy store: it charges while the switch is on and then forces its current into the output when the switch opens, which is what lifts the voltage. q0276.short: "When the boost switch opens, the inductor current has to continue, so its voltage reverses and the switch node rises until the diode conducts. q0277.title: LDO meaning and dropout advantage
q0277.short: "LDO means low-dropout regulator, a linear regulator that can keep regulating with only a small difference between input and output. Dropout is the minimum V{in}-V{out} it needs, like 200 mV at 500 mA for a MOSFET pass device, roughly load current times R{DS(on)}. q0278.title: How an LDO works
q0278.short: "It's a pass transistor in series with the load plus a feedback loop. A divider scales the output down to a feedback voltage, an error amplifier compares it with a reference and drives the pass transistor's gate. If the output sags, the amp turns the transistor on harder; if it rises, it backs off. In steady state the feedback equals the reference, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). q0279.title: LDO as a variable series resistor
q0279.short: "A variable series resistor. The pass transistor drops V{in}-V{out} at the load current, so it looks like R=(V{in}-V{out})/I{out}, and the feedback loop keeps adjusting that value to hold the output constant. So the loss is I^2R=(V{in}-V{out})I{out} and the efficiency is V{out}/V{in}. In dropout it bottoms out at R{DS(on)}. At AC, the loop makes the output impedance look inductive over its bandwidth."

q0280.title: LDO trade-offs vs step-down regulators
q0280.short: "LDOs are simple, quiet and small, with fast transient response and no EMI, but their efficiency is V{out}/V{in} and the lost power is heat, so they only work at small headroom or low current. q0281.title: External parts an LDO needs
q0281.short: "An input capacitor close to the IN pin, an output capacitor close to the OUT pin with the value and ESR the datasheet requires because it's part of the loop, and for adjustable parts two feedback resistors. Optionally an enable connection, a pull-up on power-good, a noise-reduction or soft-start capacitor, a feed-forward cap, reverse-current protection, and copper for heat. I'd check ceramics for DC-bias derating."

q0282.title: Where LDO power loss goes
q0282.short: "It becomes heat in the pass transistor: (V{in}-V{out})\times I{out} plus V{in}IQ. 5 V to 3.3 V at 500 mA is 0.85 W. q0283.title: LDO efficiency vs current and dropout
q0283.short: "Efficiency is V{out}I{out}/[V{in}(I{out}+IQ)], essentially V{out}/V{in} when the load is much bigger than IQ, so it's flat versus load current. q0284.title: How a charge pump works
q0284.short: "A charge pump uses switches and capacitors, no inductor. In phase one a flying capacitor is charged to V{in}. In phase two it's re-wired in series with the input and dumps its charge into the output capacitor, so the output is about 2V{in}. Input current is roughly twice the output current, and the output droops with load like 2V{in}-I{out}R{out}, where R{out} depends on 1/(fC) and the switch resistance."

q0285.title: How a charge pump raises voltage
q0285.short: "It's series stacking. Charge a capacitor to V{in}, then in the next phase put its bottom plate on V{in}, so its top plate is at 2V{in}, and connect that to the output. Energy is conserved because the input supplies charge twice per cycle but the output only gets it once: input current is twice output current. More stages stack more clock swings, about (N+1)V{in}, at the price of more droop and diode drops."

q0286.title: Drawing a charge pump circuit
q0286.short: "Voltage doubler: flying capacitor in the middle. S1 connects its top plate to V{in} and S2 its bottom plate to ground in phase one, charging it to V{in}. In phase two S3 connects the bottom plate to V{in} and S4 connects the top plate to the output, so the output is 2V{in}. Output capacitor and load to ground. Non-overlapping clocks. The passive version uses two diodes and a clock-driven capacitor."

q0287.title: What charge pumps are used for
q0287.short: "Anywhere I need a voltage outside the supply at low current without an inductor: negative rails from a positive supply, RS-232 levels, white-LED backlight and flash drivers with 1x/1.5x/2x modes, gate drive above the rail, and on-chip high voltage for flash programming. q0288.short: "Input current is n times output current, so ideal efficiency is V{out}/(nV{in}). q0297.short: "Lithium-ion, packaged as lithium polymer pouch cells in phones and wearables, and as cylindrical cells like the 18650 in laptops and tools. q0303.short: "Internal resistance is the series resistance inside the cell, so the terminal voltage is the open-circuit voltage minus I times R. q0322.short: "Per-cell voltage, current, temperature and time. Each cell must stay at or below 4.2 volts and I watch the spread in a series pack. q0323.short: "I'd gather requirements, then use a charger IC with power path from USB, a battery with a protection IC and dual MOSFETs, and a buck-boost or LDO to the load, plus an NTC and optionally a fuel gauge. q0324.short: "Storage charge is the level you leave a LiPo at when it's not in use, about 3.8 volts per cell, roughly 50 percent. Full charge accelerates calendar aging and gas, especially when warm, and leaves more stored energy if something fails. q0325.title: Why charging and monitoring ICs matter
q0325.short: "A lithium cell has a very tight safe window: about 4.2 V per cell within a percent or so, limited current, and a temperature range for charging. A charger IC enforces that automatically with CC/CV control, precharge for deep-discharged cells, termination, a safety timer and NTC temperature checks. q0326.short: "Balance charging makes every cell in a series pack finish at the same voltage, not just the pack total. q0327.title: Dangers of lithium batteries and prevention
q0327.short: "The main danger is thermal runaway. Lithium cells have a flammable electrolyte and a lot of stored energy, and abuse like overcharge, overdischarge, shorting, puncture or heat makes them self-heat until they vent and burn, sometimes with toxic gas. q0328.title: Handling and disposing of LiPos
q0328.short: "LiPos are soft pouch cells holding a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte, so puncture, crush, heat or shorted terminals can start an internal short and thermal runaway, even hours later. So I store them insulated, at a partial charge, cool, in a fire-safe bag, charge them only with the right charger and never unattended, and retire swollen ones. q0329.title: Why puncturing a LiPo is dangerous
q0329.short: "A LiPo is a thin stack of electrodes separated by a micron-scale separator in a soft foil pouch. A puncture bridges the electrodes, creating an internal short: the cell's energy dumps through a tiny spot, heating it fast, melting the separator and starting thermal runaway. q0330.title: LiPo overcharge and overdischarge damage
q0330.short: "Overcharging above about 4.2 volts pulls too much lithium out of the cathode, plates lithium on the anode and oxidizes the electrolyte, so you get gas, swelling, heat and potentially thermal runaway. q0331.short: "A LiPo has milliohm-level internal resistance, so a short is limited almost only by that: one 4.2 V cell at 50 milliohms gives about 84 amps, and a 4S hobby pack with 20 milliohms gives around 840. q0332.short: "Heat is a concern for three reasons. Current through the cell's internal resistance makes I squared R heat inside a small sealed package. Higher temperature speeds up the side reactions that age the cell, roughly doubling degradation per 10 degrees as a rule of thumb. q0333.title: What motors and solenoids are, and uses
q0333.short: "A motor converts electrical energy into rotation and a solenoid converts it into a short linear push or pull, both using a coil that creates a magnetic field. A solenoid is a coil with a movable plunger and a spring, good for locks, valves and relays. q0334.title: How motors and solenoids work
q0334.short: "Both use the fact that current makes a magnetic field and a field pushes on current. A solenoid is a coil with an iron plunger that the field pulls in to close the air gap, with a spring to return it; force grows with turns times current and gets much stronger as the gap shrinks. q0335.short: "A coil multiplies the magnetic effect of the current: each turn carries the same current and their fields add in the same direction inside the coil, so field and force scale with ampere-turns NI, and iron inside makes it far stronger. q0336.title: When a motor or solenoid draws most current
q0336.short: "A motor draws the most current when it's stalled or just starting, because there's no back-EMF to oppose the supply: I equals V minus Ke omega over R, so at zero speed it's V over R, say 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm, versus half an amp at free-running speed. q0337.short: "For a motor, the steady-state minimum is at no load and top speed: the back-EMF almost equals the supply, so the current is just what's needed to overcome friction, about half an amp versus 12 amps at stall in my example. q0338.short: "At steady state the inductor drops nothing, so the winding is its resistance plus back-EMF. q0339.title: Motors and solenoids as electrical loads
q0339.short: "Motors and solenoids are inductive loads: a coil resistance in series with an inductance, plus for a motor a back-EMF that depends on speed. The inductance means the current can't change instantly, so it ramps with L over R and, when you switch off, the stored energy causes a voltage spike across the switch, so you need a flyback diode or snubber. In AC the current lags the voltage, giving a power factor below one.

q0340.title: Flyback voltage
q0340.short: "Flyback voltage is the spike you get when you interrupt current in an inductive load. Since v equals L di dt, when the switch opens the coil forces its current to keep flowing and generates whatever reverse voltage it takes, limited only by parasitic capacitance or breakdown, so it can destroy the switch. q0341.title: What back EMF is
q0341.short: "Back-EMF is the voltage a spinning motor generates: a coil moving in a magnetic field induces a voltage proportional to speed, e equals Ke omega, and by Lenz's law it opposes the supply. So the current is V minus back-EMF over R: huge at stall, small at speed, and voltage essentially sets speed while current sets torque. q0342.short: "Not instantly, and for a motor usually not at all. Twelve amps is V over R, the limit. q0343.short: "Inrush current is the surge a load draws when first switched on, above its steady running current. For a motor it's because at standstill there's no back-EMF, so only the winding resistance limits the current, roughly V over R, 12 amps for a 12 volt, 1 ohm motor versus maybe 5 amps running; it lasts until the rotor speeds up. q0344.short: "A motor's current is V minus Ke omega over R, so it peaks when speed is low relative to the supply: startup, stall, jams and heavy load, V over R, so 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm. q0346.short: "A motor and a generator are the same machine with the energy flowing in opposite directions. A motor converts electrical power to mechanical: current in the field makes torque. q0347.short: "Both are coils that turn current into mechanical force and both are inductive loads that need flyback protection. q0348.short: "A brushed DC motor has a stator that doesn't move: the housing, the permanent magnets or field windings, the end caps, the brush holders and the brushes. q0349.short: "Brushed DC: simple, cheap, voltage sets speed, good for toys, pumps and automotive actuators. q0350.short: "A linear motor is a rotary motor unrolled flat: a magnet track and a coil carrier, the forcer, that moves along it. q0357.short: "Brushes are the stationary conductive contacts, usually carbon, spring-pressed against the commutator on the rotor. q0361.short: "It depends on serviceability, condition and cost. q0362.short: "Springs push the brushes onto the commutator. q0363.short: "A BLDC motor has permanent magnets on the rotor and three coils on the stator, so there's no brush or commutator. q0366.short: "Brushed motors commutate mechanically; brushless motors commutate electronically, and nearly every advantage follows from that. q0369.short: "An ESC is the electronics that sits between a battery and a motor and converts a throttle command into power for the motor. q0376.short: "A stepper is a brushless motor that moves in fixed angular steps, one per pulse to the driver, so you can position it by counting pulses, usually open loop.
