A gearbox trades motor speed for torque. Push on the shaft and the erro

q0385.title: Servo motor applications
q0385.short: "Servos go wherever something has to be at a position or follow a trajectory and hold it against load: RC steering and control surfaces, robot arm joints, camera pan-tilts and gimbals, CNC and 3D printer axes, pick-and-place machines, throttle and valve actuators. I'd use a servo when I need angle or trajectory with disturbance rejection. A plain motor is for constant speed and a solenoid for on-off strokes. Sizing s

q0386.title: Servo advantages over other motors
q0386.short: "A servo's advantage is feedback: it knows where it is, so it's accurate under any load, holds position by pushing back and reports when it fails to arrive. Its torque stays flat out to rated speed with brief higher peaks, whereas a stepper's torque falls with speed. It's efficient because current follows load, while a stepper burns full current at rest. Disadvantages are cost, complexity and tuning, so I'd pick a st

q0387.title: Controlling a servo from an MCU
q0387.short: "I generate a 50 Hz pulse with the MCU's hardware timer, 1 to 2 ms wide, e.g. 1 MHz tick, period 20,000, compare 1000 to 2000. The servo gets its own 5 to 6 V supply sized for stall current, with a bulk capacitor near it, because the MCU can't supply those spikes. Grounds are common, and I put a few hundred ohms in series with the signal. For a DIY servo from a DC motor I'd add an H-bridge, encoder and a PID loop."

q0388.title: How to spec a servo motor
q0388.short: "I'd work from the load: compute the motion profile, then peak torque as inertia times acceleration plus friction and gravity, and RMS torque for thermal duty. Pick a gear ratio, remembering reflected inertia drops as N squared. Check the motor's torque-speed curve covers the peak and the RMS is below continuous with margin. Then supply voltage and current, feedback resolution, size and environment. For a hobby servo

q0389.title: Why servos are so precise
q0389.short: "A servo is precise because it measures the shaft position and keeps correcting the error, so precision comes from the sensor and loop, not the motor. A high-resolution encoder, say 17 bits is about 0.003 degrees, gearing that makes output steps finer, high loop gain for stiffness and an integral term that drives steady-state error to zero. Resolution isn't accuracy though: backlash, flex, friction and sensor error s

q0390.title: Motor and solenoid failure modes
q0390.short: "Main failure modes are thermal, electrical and mechanical. Stall or overload makes current V over R, and the winding overheats in seconds, so use current limiting, thermal protection and stall detection. Switching off the coil produces an inductive spike that kills drivers, so use a flyback diode or snubber. Brushes, bearings and plungers wear or stick, and solenoids burn out if held on beyond their duty cycle, so p

q0391.title: Dangers of motors and solenoids
q0391.short: "Dangers are to people, equipment and the system. People: pinching and entanglement, a 20 kg·cm servo gives about 100 N at 2 cm; unexpected restart after a reset; burns from stalled motors; shock from mains or high-voltage supplies; fire from battery shorts. Equipment: inductive spikes that kill drivers, regeneration that raises the supply, stall overheating. Mitigation: low voltage, guards, torque and current limits

q0392.title: What to measure on a motor or solenoid
q0392.short: "I'd measure by purpose. Protection: current, winding temperature and supply voltage. Control: speed and position from an encoder or back-EMF, and torque, which comes from current since torque is about Kt times current. Health: input power, efficiency, vibration, and trends like winding resistance, which also gives temperature. For solenoids I'd add the current waveform and stroke time to know whether the plunger act

q0393.title: Monitoring a motor with sensors
q0393.short: "One chain per quantity. Current: low-value shunt, current-sense amplifier and ADC, with a comparator for fast trips, or a Hall sensor if I need isolation. Temperature: NTC thermistor on the housing through a divider, RTD or thermocouple for accuracy or range, IR if contactless. Speed and position: encoder or Hall sensors into a timer. Bus voltage: divider to ADC. Vibration: accelerometer. I'd synchronise sampling to

q0394.title: Acting on motor monitoring data
q0394.short: "I'd match the response to severity. Shorts trip a hardware comparator immediately. Overcurrent gets cycle-by-cycle limiting. Slow overload and heat use an I squared t or thermal model to derate smoothly, then shut down with hysteresis. Stall, meaning high current and no motion for a set time, stops the drive, retries a few times and latches. I'd also compensate for supply droop, limit decel to avoid regeneration, ru

q0395.title: Measuring motor or solenoid current
q0395.short: "Most commonly a milliohm-scale shunt resistor plus a current-sense amplifier into the ADC: 20 A through 2 mΩ is 40 mV, gain 75 gives 3 V. Low-side is simple but only sees on-time current; high-side or in-line sees more but needs a high-common-mode amplifier. Hall sensors give isolation, MOSFET RDS(on) sensing saves a part but drifts with temperature. Because PWM chops the current I sample mid on-time or filter, and

q0396.title: Detecting motor or solenoid temperature
q0396.short: "The common options are an NTC thermistor in a divider, cheap and sensitive, an RTD like Pt100 for accuracy, a thermocouple for high temperatures, or an IC sensor for board temperature. For protection a thermal fuse or bimetal switch needs no electronics. And since copper resistance rises about 0.4 percent per kelvin, I can infer average winding temperature from its resistance. I'd embed the sensor in the winding if

q0397.title: Which motor temperatures matter
q0397.short: "Several temperatures matter. The winding, average and hot spot, limits insulation life, so I embed a thermistor or use resistance. The stator and housing lag but are easy to measure. For permanent-magnet motors the rotor magnets matter: NdFeB loses about 0.1 percent flux per kelvin and can demagnetise, but you can't sense it directly, so I estimate it. Bearings have a grease limit, brushes wear, and the MOSFET junct

q0398.title: Contactless temperature of moving motors
q0398.short: "Infrared: a thermopile sensor or IR thermometer reads the surface from a distance, and a thermal camera gives an image. The catch is emissivity: black or painted surfaces are around 0.95 but shiny metal might be 0.1, so a bare shaft at 100 °C can read about 36 °C. Fix with matte tape or paint. Without optics, I can infer temperature from winding resistance or back-EMF constant, use a thermal model, or use telemetry

q0399.title: How motors degrade with age
q0399.short: "Motors drift as they age. Bearings wear and grease degrades, so friction and no-load current rise, with more noise and heat. Brushes shorten and the commutator grooves, increasing contact resistance and sparking. Insulation ages and can short turns; magnets can lose strength, lowering the torque constant so you need more current per newton-metre. Efficiency falls, a 73 percent motor might drop to 61. Reliability fol

q0400.title: Stresses on a motor over its life
q0400.short: "Four groups. Thermal: steady heat ages insulation and cycling fatigues joints. Electrical: inrush is V over R, so a 12 V, 1.2 ohm motor sees 10 A at start, 25 times the heating of a 2 A run; plugging can double stall current; plus inductive spikes and PWM edges stressing insulation and bearings. Mechanical: start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, overspeed. Environmental: moisture, dust, chemicals. I'd soft-start,

q0401.title: Thin coil wire versus high current
q0401.short: "The premise is off: many turns of thin wire gives higher resistance and lower current, and force depends on ampere-turns, so you pick turns to match your supply. 4500 turns of 0.12 mm wire draws about 45 mA at 12 V. Large currents occur only at start, stall or overload; a running motor's back-EMF limits current, and solenoids are rated by duty cycle. Coils don't always burn out; they fail when heat outruns cooling,

q0402.title: Why measure motor/solenoid speed and position
q0402.short: "Voltage only sets what a motor tries to do. Load, supply and temperature change what it actually does, so for speed control, positioning, BLDC commutation, stall and jam detection and diagnostics you need to measure speed or position and close the loop. For a solenoid the equivalent is knowing the plunger arrived, how hard it hit, and whether it jammed, so you can drop to a hold current, soften the landing and flag

q0403.title: Measuring motor RPM
q0403.short: "I'd get a pulse train from an encoder, a Hall sensor on a magnet, or an optical interrupter, and convert with rpm equals 60 times frequency divided by pulses per rev. At high speed I count pulses in a fixed window; at low speed I time the period between pulses with a hardware timer. No sensor? Back-EMF is proportional to speed, so I can measure terminal voltage during a PWM off-time. For lab checks I'd use an optica

q0404.title: Determining motor position
q0404.short: "I'd pick between absolute and incremental. Absolute options are a potentiometer, a magnetic angle sensor (12 bits or more, contactless) or an absolute encoder. Incremental means an optical quadrature encoder, which needs homing at power-up. Brushless motors have Hall sensors good for commutation (about 60 electrical degrees). Steppers count steps if they don't slip. The gear ratio multiplies output resolution but ad

q0405.title: Rotary encoder and speed measurement
q0405.short: "A rotary encoder converts shaft rotation into electrical pulses. An incremental quadrature encoder gives two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees apart, so the phase order gives direction and counting every edge gives four times the line count, plus an index pulse once per rev. For speed I count edges over a fixed window, rpm equals 60 times counts over CPR times window, or time between edges at low speed. Absolute enc

q0406.title: Measuring solenoid speed
q0406.short: "I'd time the plunger between two known points: optical or Hall gates a set distance apart, velocity equals distance over time, with a hardware timer. Or I differentiate a position sensor like a linear Hall or LVDT, with filtering. Without a sensor, the coil gives velocity through the motional back-EMF, i\,dL/dx\,v, which makes a dip in the current during the stroke. Lab check with a high-speed camera or laser."

q0407.title: Measuring solenoid position
q0407.short: "For just home or extended, a limit switch, reed or Hall switch. For continuous position: a linear Hall sensor with a magnet on the plunger (nonlinear, so linearise), an LVDT (precise, contactless, needs excitation), a linear pot, or an optical strip. Sensorless: inductance depends on air gap, so a small test pulse measures L and hence position, best near the closed end. I'd pick on resolution, linearity, temperature

q0408.title: BEMF speed sensing for motors and solenoids
q0408.short: "Back-EMF is proportional to speed, E equals Ke omega. The terminal voltage is IR plus L di/dt plus E, so I measure it when the current is zero: switch the drive off during the PWM off-time, wait for the freewheel current to decay, and sample the terminal through a divider into an ADC. Speed is that voltage over Ke. Otherwise subtract the I times R drop during on-time. It fails at low speed and drifts with temperatur

q0409.title: How to drive an inductive load
q0409.short: "I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch with the load between the supply and the drain, a gate resistor and pull-down, and a flyback diode across the load so the inductor current has a path when the FET turns off. Size the FET for voltage margin and stall or inrush current, then use PWM for speed or hold current. For two directions or protection and diagnostics, step up to an H-bridge or a driver IC."

q0410.title: Adding motor braking to a drive
q0410.short: "A single low-side switch can only coast. To brake I give the motor's back-EMF a short-circuit path: in a half-bridge, turn on the low-side FET; in an H-bridge, turn on both low sides. The motor then acts as a generator into its own resistance and stops in a time constant of tens of milliseconds instead of seconds. I'd check the brake current, E over R, against FET and winding ratings, limit it with PWM if needed, an

q0411.title: Driving a motor in both directions
q0411.short: "An H-bridge: four switches around the motor. Turning on the top-left and bottom-right sends current one way; top-right and bottom-left the other way. PWM one switch for speed. Never turn on both switches of one leg, so I add dead time or use a driver IC with shoot-through protection. Body diodes carry freewheel current, both low sides give braking, all off is coast. The MCU drives it with PWM plus a direction pin or

q0412.title: Kinds of motor braking
q0412.short: "Five kinds: coast, which is just letting friction work; dynamic braking, shorting the terminals or adding a resistor so the motor dissipates its energy as a generator; plugging, reversing the voltage for the fastest stop at high current; regenerative braking, returning energy to the supply with a bridge; and mechanical brakes for holding torque and fail-safe. Electrical braking loses torque as speed drops, so combin

q0413.title: Protection for inductive load drives
q0413.short: "Layers. For the kick, a flyback diode, or a diode plus Zener or TVS for faster release. For the gate, a series resistor, pull-down and maybe a gate Zener. For over-current, a sense resistor with current limit, plus a fuse; motors stall at V over R. Thermal shutdown. On the supply side, reverse-polarity protection, a TVS for surges and bulk capacitance for regeneration. In bridges, dead time. Plus a capacitor across

q0414.title: Drive switch trade-offs: EMR, SSR, MOSFET, BJT, IGBT
q0414.short: "Relay: contacts, zero on-state loss, isolation, AC or DC, but slow, wears, can't PWM, and DC inductive arcs hurt. SSR: isolated, silent, but about a volt drop (triac types) and AC-only unless MOSFET-based. MOSFET: voltage-driven, milliohm resistance, fast, the default for low-voltage PWM. BJT: cheap, current-driven, 0.2 to 0.7 V drop. IGBT: high voltage and current with constant drop, slower. 12 V motor: MOSFET. Mai

q0415.title: Faster solenoid drive: velocity and cycle rate
q0415.short: "Cycle time is pull-in plus release plus return. For pull-in I over-excite: a high voltage for the first few milliseconds, then PWM down to a hold current, since force goes as current squared and a closed plunger needs much less. For release I replace the plain flyback diode with a Zener or TVS so the coil sees a high reverse voltage and the current collapses fast. Add soft landing to stop bounce, and mechanical twea

q0416.title: Specifying a motor/solenoid driver IC
q0416.short: "I'd start from the motor's supply range including transients, stall and running current. Then check the IC's operating voltage with headroom, continuous current thermally using hot R{DS(on)} and R{\theta JA}, peak or limit above inrush, then features: interface and logic level, PWM frequency, current regulation, decay modes, protections (OCP, OTP, UVLO, shoot-through, fault pin), sleep current, package and cost. Fin

q0417.title: Specifying discrete transistors for a drive
q0417.short: "Voltage: at least twice the supply plus clamp, e.g. 40 V on a 12 V rail. Current: size from stall or the current limit, but the real limit is heat, so use hot R{DS(on)} at my actual gate voltage, which means logic-level for 3.3 or 5 V drive, and compute I^2R plus switching and gate loss against thermal resistance. Then gate charge and the Q{gd}/Q{gs} ratio for drive and Miller immunity, SOA or avalanche if unclamped

q0418.title: What limits switching frequency
q0418.short: "Mainly loss and timing. Switching loss, half V I times rise-plus-fall time times f, plus gate-drive, C{oss} and diode recovery losses, all scale with frequency and add to conduction loss until the thermal limit. Then dead time, minimum on-time and blanking eat a bigger share of a shorter period, gate drivers can only supply so much current, and the timer resolution caps the frequency. EMI rises too. The lower bound

q0419.title: Increasing the switching frequency
q0419.short: "I'd cut each limiter: shorten the switching edges with a stronger gate driver, lower Rg and low-Q{gd} FETs, tighten the layout to keep ringing down, use synchronous rectification to kill diode recovery, and go to GaN or SiC if I need MHz. Reduce dead time and blanking, give the timer resolution, and manage EMI and heat. For a motor, I might not raise the device frequency at all: a unipolar bridge or interleaving dou

q0420.title: Draw an H-bridge circuit
q0420.short: "An H-bridge is two half-bridges: each leg has a high-side and a low-side switch, and the motor sits between the two middle nodes. Turn on top-left plus bottom-right and current flows one way; top-right plus bottom-left reverses it; both low sides shorts the motor for braking; all off lets it coast. With MOSFETs I draw NFETs low and PFETs, or bootstrapped NFETs, high, include the body diodes for the inductive freewhe

q0421.title: Draw a half-bridge circuit
q0421.short: "A half-bridge is two switches in series from the supply to ground, with the output at the middle node. High side on gives the supply, low side on gives ground, both off lets an inductive load clamp through a body diode. I'd use two NFETs with body diodes, a bootstrapped gate driver for the high side, and dead time so the two never overlap. The average output is duty cycle times supply, and with an LC filter it becom

q0422.title: How a half/H-bridge works
q0422.short: "A half-bridge connects the output to the supply or to ground, and PWM duty sets the average output. The inductive motor current can't stop when the top switch opens, so it freewheels through the bottom FET or its body diode. An H-bridge is two half-bridges with the motor in between: one leg high and the other low gives one direction, the opposite gives reverse, and PWM on one leg, or on both in anti-phase, sets spee

q0423.title: H-bridge vs half-bridge trade-offs
q0423.short: "A half-bridge is one leg of two FETs; it drives a load between its output and a fixed rail, so the load sees zero to the supply and a motor only turns one way. An H-bridge is two legs with the load floating between them, which gives plus or minus the full supply, so reverse, brake and regeneration, but it needs twice the FETs and drivers, and has twice the conduction loss. Use a half-bridge for fans, solenoids and b

q0424.title: Braking a motor with half/H-bridges
q0424.short: "I'd brake with a half-bridge by turning on the low-side FET, which ties both motor terminals to ground, so the back-EMF drives current through the winding and the motor slows. An H-bridge can do that with both low sides, or can plug by applying reverse voltage, which makes current (V+E)/R, about twice as much, and stops several times faster. The stress is peak current, winding heating, a torque jolt on the gears and

q0425.title: Asymmetrical half-bridge vs symmetrical H-bridge
q0425.short: "An asymmetrical half-bridge is one where the two FETs differ or where the load only sees one polarity, so I'd use it for unidirectional loads and buck converters at lopsided duty cycles; resizing the FETs to match the duty cycle cuts conduction loss, 20% at D = 0.1. I need a symmetrical H-bridge when the load must see both polarities or zero DC average: reversing motors, voice coils, class-D speakers and transformer

q0426.title: High-side NFET advantages and challenges
q0426.short: "An NFET is the better switch because electrons are two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same die it has lower on-resistance and gate charge, and it's cheaper with more choices. The challenge on the high side is that its source is the switch node, so the gate has to be a few volts above the supply, which needs a floating gate supply: a bootstrap capacitor or charge pump. That limits duty cycle and co

q0427.title: Drive circuit for a high-side NFET
q0427.short: "A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 V above its source, and the source is the switch node, so I need a gate supply that floats with it. I'd use a half-bridge driver with a bootstrap: a fast diode from the 10 V supply to a capacitor that sits between the boot pin and the switch node. It charges when the low side is on and lifts the gate drive when the high side turns on. Size it as gate charge over allowed droop

q0428.title: PFET and NFET on together: shoot-through
q0428.short: "Turning on the PFET and NFET in the same leg shorts the supply to ground through two on-resistances, so you get big current spikes, heat, rail droop and often a dead FET. It happens with overlapping gate edges, tied gates, mismatched turn-off and turn-on delays, or Miller-coupled dv/dt. I prevent it with separate gate drives and dead time, a driver with built-in shoot-through protection, faster turn-off than turn-on

q0429.title: Drive an inductive load from a GPIO
q0429.short: "I'd use a low-side logic-level N-channel MOSFET: load from the supply to the drain, source to ground, GPIO to the gate. A flyback diode across the load takes the inductive kick, a 100 k pull-down on the gate keeps it off when the MCU is in reset, a 100 to 220 Ω series gate resistor limits GPIO current and ringing, and a bulk capacitor supports the supply. If the load is on a different or noisy supply, add isolation

q0430.title: Why a gate pulldown resistor
q0430.short: "A MOSFET gate is a capacitor with a huge DC resistance, so if the driving pin is in reset, booting or set as an input, the gate floats and drifts with leakage and noise, and can drift above threshold. Then the FET half-turns on and either fires the load at power-up or sits in its linear region burning power. A 10 to 100 kΩ pulldown from gate to source gives the gate a defined path to ground so it defaults off, and c

q0431.title: Gate series resistor and parasitic oscillation
q0431.short: "The gate is a capacitor, and the wire and package feeding it add nanohenries of inductance, so a fast driver edge makes a series LC that rings at tens of megahertz and overshoots the gate; with enough gain and feedback through the Miller capacitance it can even oscillate. A series gate resistor damps the loop, requiring R\ge2\sqrt{L/C}, caps the GPIO's peak current, and slows the edge to cut dv/dt and EMI, at the co

q0432.title: Why isolation matters, and its trade-offs
q0432.short: "Isolation matters for safety (keeping hazardous voltage away from people and logic), for protection (a shorted FET can't put the motor rail on the MCU pin), and for noise, because switching current on a shared ground shifts the MCU's reference by volts. It also gives floating references for high-side drives and sensors. The trade-offs are cost, area, an isolated power supply, delay and limited bandwidth, optocoupler

q0433.title: Which kinds of isolation to use
q0433.short: "It depends on what crosses the barrier and how strong it needs to be. For logic and PWM I'd use a digital isolator, or an optocoupler if it's slow. For a high-voltage bridge, an isolated gate driver with an isolated supply. For motor current sensing, an isolated amplifier or delta-sigma modulator. For buses like CAN or RS-485, an isolated transceiver, and for power, an isolated DC-DC. The grade is set by the standar

q0434.title: Opto-isolation and its trade-offs
q0434.short: "An optocoupler is an LED and a photodetector, usually a phototransistor, in one package with an insulating gap, so only light crosses and the two sides are galvanically isolated. The key spec is CTR, output current over LED current, which varies with temperature and drops with age. Trade-offs: slow with distorted pulse widths, milliamps of input current, limited common-mode immunity, and aging, in return for low cos

q0435.title: Design an opto-isolated gate drive
q0435.short: "I'd bias the LED at about 10 mA from the GPIO: (3.3 − 1.2)/10 mA is 210 Ω, so 200 Ω, active-high so reset means off. On the output side I'd run the phototransistor from an isolated 12 V as an emitter follower into a pulldown, which is non-inverting, defaults off and goes to about 11 V at end-of-life CTR, then buffer it with an NPN/PNP pair into a 10 Ω gate resistor with a gate-source pulldown, because a plain pull-u

q0436.title: What is galvanic isolation?
q0436.short: "Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path, so no DC current, yet they still exchange signal or power through light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a capacitor. It lets the two sides sit at completely different voltages, breaks ground loops and contains faults. But the barrier has a little capacitance, so fast common-mode transients still cross, it has a finite voltage rating,

q0439.title: Ways to measure current
q0439.short: "You convert current to a voltage. The common ways are a series sense resistor with an amplifier, which is cheap, accurate and DC-capable but dissipates power; using an existing resistance like a MOSFET's Rds(on) or inductor DCR, which is free but inaccurate; and magnetic sensing, Hall sensors or current transformers, which give isolation and low loss but cost more and drift. For a low-voltage board I'd default to a

q0440.title: Why measure current
q0440.short: "Four reasons. Protection, because current is what overheats and destroys hardware, so you need a fast overcurrent trip. Control, because converters use inductor current for current-mode control and motors produce torque proportional to current. Monitoring, because integrating current gives battery state of charge and multiplying by voltage gives power. And diagnostics, like detecting a stalled motor or missing load.

q0441.title: Magnetic current sensing pros and cons
q0441.short: "Magnetic sensing measures the field around the conductor instead of a voltage drop. Hall sensors detect the field directly and work at DC and AC. Current transformers and Rogowski coils use Faraday induction, so they only see AC. The big advantages are isolation, almost no insertion loss and high current range. The downsides are cost, size, offset and temperature drift, sensitivity to stray fields, and poor accuracy

q0442.title: Current sensing tradeoffs compared
q0442.short: "A shunt plus current-sense amp is the accurate, cheap, DC-capable default, but it dissipates I-squared-R and has no isolation. Rds(on) or inductor DCR sensing is lossless and free but only 10 to 20 percent accurate, so it's for protection. Hall and CT sensors give isolation, no loss and high current range, but cost more, drift, and are poor at low current, and CTs are AC only. I'd choose by current level, isolation

q0443.title: How a sense resistor works
q0443.short: "A sense resistor is a small precise resistor in series with the load. All the load current flows through it, so the voltage across it is I \times R. I measure that millivolt-level drop with a current sense amplifier and an ADC and divide by the resistance to get current. It's small to limit loss, a few milliohms, and I connect the sense lines directly to its pads, Kelvin style, so only the resistor is in the measure

q0444.title: Sense resistor pros and cons
q0444.short: "Sense resistors are cheap, small, linear and accurate, they work from DC to high frequency, and they handle overloads. The downsides are that they dissipate I^2R and drop voltage so they don't scale to very high current, their tiny signal means amplifier offset limits low-current accuracy, resistance drifts with temperature, parasitic inductance corrupts fast edges, and there's no isolation. They also need Kelvin ro

q0445.title: Specifying a sense resistor
q0445.short: "I find the allowed window for the resistance. The upper limit is set by voltage drop and power at maximum current, R \le \min(V{drop}/I{max}, P/I{max}^2). The lower limit is set by the smallest current I need to measure: the signal must beat amplifier offset, so R \ge V{os}/(\varepsilon I{min}). Then I pick a low-TCR, low-ESL part rated at least twice the dissipation. Too big wastes power and drops voltage; too smal

q0446.title: Sense resistor from ADC range
q0446.short: "I take the ADC full-scale voltage, divide by the maximum current with about 10 percent headroom, and that gives the largest resistor: Rs = V{FS}/(1.1 I{max}). Then I check power I^2R, voltage drop, and resolution per LSB. If the result is silly, like 27 ohms at 100 milliamps, I use a small shunt and an amplifier instead. For bidirectional current I use half the range, since zero sits at mid-scale."

q0447.title: High-side vs low-side current sensing
q0447.short: "Low-side puts the shunt between load and ground: simple, cheap, near-zero common-mode, but it lifts the load's ground by IRs and can't see a short-to-ground fault. High-side puts it between supply and load: load stays grounded and short-to-ground is detected, but the amplifier must handle bus-level common-mode voltage and have good CMRR. I use high-side when the load must be grounded or for protection, and low-side

q0448.title: Sensing current with MOSFET Vds
q0448.short: "A fully-on MOSFET is a small resistor, so I = V{DS}/R{DS(on)}. You measure drain-source voltage with a comparator or amplifier and get current with no added loss, part or board space, which is why it's used for overcurrent protection. The cons are accuracy: R{DS(on)} rises 50 percent or more when hot and varies part to part, it only works while the FET is fully on and after the switching edge settles, and the signal

q0449.title: What a current sense amplifier is
q0449.short: "A current sense amplifier takes the small voltage across a shunt, rejects the large common-mode bus voltage it sits on, multiplies the difference by a precise fixed gain like 20 or 50, and outputs a ground-referenced voltage for an ADC or comparator, often with a reference pin for bidirectional current. Inside it's a difference amplifier with trimmed matched resistors, so V{out} = G\,I\,R{sense} + V{ref}. Key specs

q0450.title: When you need a CSA

q0460.short: "A PCB is an insulating board, usually fibreglass-epoxy FR-4, with copper traces etched on it that connect components soldered to pads.
